meaning: Relaxed and unbothered about having to work; not making a fuss about the job or the effort it demands. (Reading the standard pattern 'be cool about (something)' = to take it calmly, without complaint or resentment.)
note: NOT a standard idiom as written. This looks like a phrase lifted mid-sentence or a deck slip. The real idiomatic unit is 'be cool about something' / 'be cool with something'; 'working' is just whatever noun happened to follow it. Meaning above is the transparent reading, not a dictionary idiom.

meaning: Drew upon his imagination rather than on fact — invented or made up the material out of his own head. 'Fancy' here is the older sense of 'imagination', and 'draw on' means to call upon as a resource.
note: Inflected form of 'draw on one's fancy'. Slightly literary/archaic; 'draw on one's imagination' is the modern equivalent.

meaning: Something that proves bitterly disappointing or worthless once you actually get it — a hoped-for prize that turns out hollow. Often as 'turn to dust and ashes in one's mouth'. A secondary, older sense is human insignificance or mortality (as in 'I am but dust and ashes').
note: Biblical in origin. The live idiomatic sense in modern use is 'bitter disappointment / anticlimax', not literal mortality.

meaning: To accept someone's hospitality and so become obliged and loyal to them. Usually met in the negative — 'I will not eat anyone's salt' = I will not be beholden to anyone, I will owe nobody.
note: Widely used in Indian English (compare 'namak halal' / 'namak haram' — being true or false to the salt you have eaten). The phrasing with 'anyone's' points at the negative, independence-asserting use.

meaning: CORRUPTION of 'hedge one's bets' = to protect yourself against loss by backing more than one outcome; to avoid committing fully to a single option so you cannot be badly hurt whichever way things go.
note: CORRUPT HEADING. 'Edge' is a typo for 'hedge'. 'Edge one's bets' is not an English idiom; the hedging sense comes from hedging a wager (fencing it in against loss).

meaning: Finished in complete and humiliating failure — the undertaking collapsed embarrassingly rather than merely falling short.
note: Not an idiom, and non-standard as written — normal English is 'ended in a fiasco' / 'ended in fiascos'. This reads like a phrase lifted mid-sentence with the article dropped. The meaning is transparent from 'fiasco'; there is no figurative content beyond the word itself.

meaning: Enough freedom of action for a person to bring about their own downfall. From 'give him enough rope and he'll hang himself' — do not stop someone who is going wrong; let them carry on and their own mistakes will finish them.
note: Elliptical for 'give someone enough rope'. Carries a note of deliberate, patient malice: you allow the freedom precisely because you expect self-destruction.

meaning: A person's malevolent double — a counterpart who looks the same but behaves wickedly. Used loosely for anything that imitates a legitimate thing while being harmful, and jokingly for someone acting wildly out of character ('that must have been my evil twin').
note: Modern, originally from soap-opera and comic-book plots. There is also a specific computing sense (a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot impersonating a genuine one), which is an extension of the same idea.

meaning: The harmful after-effects or repercussions of an event — the trouble that settles on people once the main incident is over (political fallout, the fallout from a scandal).
note: Figurative extension of radioactive fallout: the damage is delayed, spreads beyond the original target, and is not what anyone intended.

meaning: To sound him out — to test his opinions, mood or intentions discreetly, without declaring your own hand, before deciding how to proceed.
note: Also 'feel the pulse of' a group/market = gauge its prevailing mood. The literal medical sense is not the idiom.

meaning: Retreated; withdrew to a safer or earlier position rather than pressing on (of troops, or of a person giving ground in an argument).
note: Inflected phrasal verb lifted mid-sentence, so ambiguous: if the original was 'fell back on', the sense is quite different — 'fall back on something' = to resort to it as a reserve when the first option fails. Both are live idioms; the bare 'fell back' reads as 'retreated'.

meaning: To have done with it — to reach the point of needing or wanting it no further, so that you can put it aside or pass it on. Of a person ('finish with someone'), to break off the relationship.
note: Distinct from simply 'finish something' (complete it); 'finish WITH something' is about being done needing it, not about completing it.

meaning: Something intensely bitter and galling — a source of deep resentment and mortification, especially having to watch a rival succeed.
note: Biblical (Lamentations); gall and wormwood are both proverbially bitter substances. Typically 'it was gall and wormwood to him'.

meaning: Betrayed or revealed unintentionally — let out a secret, or let a look or gesture expose what was being concealed ('his voice gave him away').
note: Inflected form lifted mid-sentence, and 'give away' has two other live senses that the bare heading cannot distinguish: to hand over free of charge, and (of a father) to give the bride away at a wedding. The idiomatic/figurative sense is 'betray, reveal'.

meaning: To earn recognition or praise for doing something well or correctly. Frequently sarcastic — 'do you want a gold star?' belittles someone seeking credit for the trivial or the merely expected.
note: From the sticker a primary-school teacher awards for good work; the schoolroom origin is why the ironic use bites.

meaning: To obtain a university degree or diploma; to graduate.
note: Chiefly American. Diplomas were formerly written on parchment made from sheepskin, so 'sheepskin' became slang for the diploma itself.

meaning: To move or progress at the same rate as another, neither one gaining on the other.
note: This is NOT an English idiom — it reads like the DEFINITION side of a flashcard that has been used as the heading. The idioms that carry this sense are 'keep pace (with)', 'go neck and neck', or 'keep up with'. Flagging as a likely deck corruption rather than answering it as a genuine idiom.

meaning: To use it sparingly or in moderation — don't overdo it ('go easy on the salt'). With a person, 'go easy on someone' means to treat them leniently and not punish or criticise them harshly.
note: The 'on something' framing selects the 'use sparingly' sense; the 'on someone' framing selects the 'be lenient' sense. Same idiom, object decides.

meaning: To examine or review something carefully from start to finish — check it point by point, or rehearse it again.
note: Bare heading, so the other live sense is not distinguished: 'go over well / badly' = to be received in a particular way by an audience. 'Go over to' = change sides or allegiance.

meaning: CORRUPTION of 'give the green light' (or 'get the green light') = to grant, or receive, permission for something to proceed.
note: CORRUPT HEADING. 'Go the green light' is not English; the verb should be 'give' or 'get'. From traffic signals — the green light is authority to move off.

meaning: A churchyard or burial ground; a cemetery, thought of as ground belonging to God where the dead are sown to await resurrection.
note: Somewhat archaic/literary. From German 'Gottesacker', and Longfellow's poem of that title is why the phrase persists in English.

meaning: A born fool — someone made foolish by nature, an idiot from birth rather than through his own doing.
note: Archaic and rare; I am recalling this from older dictionary usage rather than from live English, so treat with care. A separate medieval theological sense also exists, in which the DEVIL is called God's ape because he mimics and counterfeits God's works. The two senses are unrelated, and a deck could legitimately intend either — this is worth checking against the source book.

meaning: Sets about a task, tackles it in a particular manner ('the way he goes about it'); or, of news and rumour, circulates and is passed around.
note: Inflected phrasal verb lifted mid-sentence; the two senses above are both common and the bare heading does not separate them. 'Go about with someone' (keep company with) is a third, older sense.

meaning: Had a good, friendly relationship with someone; also, made good progress with a task.
note: British usage; the American equivalent of the relationship sense is 'got along well'. Inflected form lifted mid-sentence.

idiom: Have the ball at your feet
meaning: To have a fine opportunity within your grasp and the power to make something of it — everything is set up for you and it is now yours to take.
note: From football: the ball is at your feet, nobody is stopping you, the chance is yours to convert or waste. Often used of a young person's prospects.

meaning: Visibly caught out — carrying the obvious evidence of your own wrongdoing or blunder, and made to look foolish by it.
note: Possible corruption of the far commoner 'egg on your face' (= made to look foolish when something you backed goes wrong). But the jam version may be genuine British usage, from a child caught with jam round the mouth after raiding the pot — which shifts the sense from 'made a fool of' toward 'caught red-handed'. Uncertain which the deck intends; flagging rather than asserting.

meaning: CORRUPTION of 'Judas kiss' = an outward show of affection or friendship that is in fact an act of betrayal.
note: CORRUPT HEADING — a clear typo for 'Judas'. 'Junda' is not a word in English. From Judas Iscariot identifying Christ to the soldiers with a kiss.

meaning: Stay calm; don't lose your temper or get agitated.
note: Variant of 'keep your hair on' (British) and 'keep your shirt on' (American). All three picture a person so enraged that the covering comes off.

meaning: Waiting about with nothing to do — idling away time, usually against his will, because he is being kept waiting by someone else.
note: Note the trap: the American 'kick up one's heels' means the opposite kind of thing — to enjoy oneself boisterously. 'Kick one's heels' (British) is frustrated idleness, not fun.

meaning: Diagonally opposite — positioned across a corner from something rather than directly beside or facing it ('the bank is kitty-corner from the post office').
note: American; a folk-altered form of 'cater-corner', also heard as 'catty-corner'. 'Cater' here is from French 'quatre' (four), i.e. across the four corners of a crossing — nothing to do with cats.

meaning: To take in eagerly and with obvious relish — especially praise, flattery or attention, accepted greedily and uncritically.
note: From an animal lapping liquid with its tongue. Usually carries a hint of disdain: the person enjoying it is being undiscriminating or vain.
